paragraphs.heading: Real part and imaginary part
paragraphs.text: A complex number is written a + bi. Here a and b are ordinary real numbers. The symbol i stands for the imaginary unit, which satisfies i² = −1. The real number a is the real part, and the real number b, not bi, is the imaginary part. For example, 2 + 3i is a complex number with real part 2 and imaginary part 3. The set of all complex numbers is written ℂ or C.

paragraphs.heading: Why they were needed
paragraphs.text: Squaring any nonzero real number gives a positive result, so for a long time taking the square root of a negative number was thought impossible. In the 16th century such roots turned out to help in finding real solutions of cubic equations, but they were seen as a mere trick with symbols, and in the 17th century they were named imaginary numbers. Despite the name, they are not made up: they are as valid as real numbers and essential for describing the physical world. With complex numbers, every non-constant polynomial equation with real or complex coefficients has a solution, even one with no real solution. This result is called the fundamental theorem of algebra.

paragraphs.heading: Doing arithmetic
paragraphs.text: Complex numbers extend the real numbers: a real number a is just a + 0i, and a purely imaginary number bi is 0 + bi. You can add, subtract, multiply and divide them, and the usual associative, commutative and distributive laws still hold, which makes the complex numbers a field. Adding and subtracting work part by part: (x + yi) + (u + vi) = (x + u) + (y + v)i, and (x + yi) − (u + vi) = (x − u) + (y − v)i.

paragraphs.heading: Numbers as points
paragraphs.text: Each complex number a + bi can be matched to the point (a, b) on a flat grid called the complex plane, or Argand diagram. The real part is usually shown along the horizontal axis, growing to the right, and the imaginary part along the vertical axis, growing upwards. This turns arithmetic into geometry. Adding a complex number slides the whole plane over, while multiplying by one scales and rotates it.

paragraphs.heading: Conjugate and size
paragraphs.text: The complex conjugate of z = x + yi is z̄ = x − yi, which is the mirror image of z across the real axis. Multiplying z by its conjugate gives x² + y², a real number that is never negative. Its square root, |z| = √(x² + y²), is called the absolute value or modulus of z. By Pythagoras' theorem, it is the distance from the origin to z in the complex plane, and the numbers with |z| = 1 make up the circle of radius one around the origin.

paragraphs.heading: Angle and another notation
paragraphs.text: The argument of z, also called its phase, is the angle of the line from the origin to z, measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis. It is fixed only up to adding integer multiples of 2π, since turning the plane by 2π, or 360°, leaves every point where it was; one possible choice keeps it within (−π, π]. With r = |z| and φ = arg z, any complex number can be written z = r(cos φ + isin φ). In electrical engineering, where i often stands for electric current, j is written instead of i.
